title: Redwood discovery - Tidal Payments latency & throughput
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency needs, and token/sec benchmarking across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private options. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share benchmark tooling and run a baseline on Hosted; schedule Dedicated POC if hosted results align.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-06
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Tidal CTO), Lena Morales (Tidal Head of ML), Roberto Diaz (Infra)

Summary: quick discovery on latency/throughput goals and whether Hosted can meet p95 targets vs Dedicated/Private. Lots of benchmarking talk and action items to run a baseline.

[00:00] Alyssa Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alyssa with Redwood, this is Marcus our SE. Quick intros?
[00:08] Samir Patel: Hey I'm Samir, CTO at Tidal Payments. We run several realtime fraud models and are trying to add a generative layer for customer support and reconciliation. Latency is our main blocker.
[00:20] Lena Morales: Hi, Lena. We care about p95 latency under load, streaming for progressive responses, and also token/sec throughput for nightly bulk jobs.
[00:33] Marcus Lee: Great, thx. Quick qual: what p95 targets are you aiming for for the interactive paths vs batch?
[00:40] Roberto Diaz: For interactive, p95 we'd like to be under 600ms for 16-64 token outputs, ideally <400ms but we can stretch. Concurrency on peak is about 200-500 concurrent streaming sessions. Batch jobs we care about tokens/sec and cost efficiency.
[01:02] Marcus Lee: OK that's helpful. On Hosted we typically see p95 in the ~200-800ms range depending on model size and prompt length; with continuous batching and prefix/KV cache we often meet 300-500ms for common open models. For Dedicated you get more predictable tail latency because of reserved GPU pools.
[01:25] Samir Patel: When you say p95 300-500ms, is that for first token or full response?
[01:30] Marcus Lee: Good question	usually p95 for first token (time to first byte/first token) for short prompts. Full response varies with token count; streaming reduces perceived latency.
[01:40] Alyssa Chen: Also worth noting our p95 numbers are measured with our benchmark harness	we'll share the script. That harness simulates your concurrency profile, sequence length distribution, and streaming chunk sizes.
[01:52] Lena Morales: Perfect. We have a lot of short responses (16-32 tokens) for IVR and chat, and longer assistants for reconciliation (~200-500 tokens) that can be backgrounded. For the short ones we need tight p95.
[02:08] Marcus Lee: For 16-32 tokens our Hosted tests on the mid-sized models (eg distil-like / small Llama variants) often hit ~250-450ms p95 at 200 concurrent when prefix cache is hot. If cache is cold tail can spike; that's where warmup and smart routing helps.
[02:29] Roberto Diaz: Curious about token/sec benchmarks. We do nightly large scale runs	want to understand tokens per sec per GPU with Redwood.
[02:36] Marcus Lee: Sure. Numbers vary a lot by model and quantization. Ballpark: on a single A100-type instance with optimized kernels you might get 1k-3k tokens/sec for generation depending on decoding strategy and beam sampling. With batching you can push higher token/sec but at the cost of per-request latency.
[02:55] Samir Patel: Right, so there's a tradeoff. For streaming we can't batch across users much, since each session streams. How does Redwood handle streaming + batching?
[03:05] Marcus Lee: We use continuous batching and dynamic windowing	small latency-sensitive requests get prioritized and batched opportunistically. For streaming we send tokens as they're generated and maintain KV cache so subsequent tokens are faster. There's also an option to favor latency in routing policies to avoid batching that adds too much delay.
[03:25] Lena Morales: You mentioned KV cache	we've heard your docs say KV cache and prefix caching. Do you support sticky sessions so a user hits the same cache location?
[03:33] Marcus Lee: Yes, you can pin sessions or use sticky routing keys. In Dedicated you can get more consistent KV locality. In Hosted we have smart routing that balances cache effectiveness with overall capacity. Occasionally the transcription	sorry the notes	say KV "cash" in older exports, that's a transcription weirdness.
[03:50] Alyssa Chen: Haha, yes the automated transcripts do that sometimes.
[03:54] Samir Patel: On the security side	VPC / Private deployment? We handle PCI data and need strict controls.
[04:00] Alyssa Chen: Understood. For PCI we usually advise Private deployment (customer VPC or on-prem) with customer-managed KMS, audit logs, SOC2 attestations. Dedicated can be in a customer VPC as well for isolation. We'll send the security pack.
[04:12] Roberto Diaz: Good. For the POC: we want to run a baseline on Hosted first to validate the model and prompts, then consider Dedicated if we need tighter SLAs. How would you recommend we run benchmarks?
[04:23] Marcus Lee: We'll share our benchmark harness (script + Docker) that simulates concurrency, streaming chunk sizes (we usually benchmark with 8 token chunks for streaming), and measures p50/p95/p99 for first token and full completion. We ask customers to provide a representative prompt set and sequence length distribution.
[04:40] Samir Patel: How do you simulate network effects? Our infra is regionally distributed, we care about egress and routing latencies.
[04:47] Marcus Lee: The harness supports adding synthetic network delay and multi-region clients. For Hosted we can run tests from a region close to your users; for Dedicated/Private the network topology is more controlled.
[04:57] Lena Morales: Do you have any published numbers for p95 at 200 concurrent with streaming enabled? Even a rough table?
[05:03] Alyssa Chen: We have internal benchmarks	I'll summarize in the follow-up. Roughly: for small-medium models on Hosted, p95 first-token at 200 concurrent with streaming is 250-500ms; large models 600-1200ms. Dedicated can reduce variance and often brings p99 down significantly. We'll send model-specific curves.
[05:22] Samir Patel: And cost tradeoffs? If we push Dedicated to reduce p95, what's the typical uplift?
[05:28] Alyssa Chen: Typically Dedicated is a fixed monthly commit plus lower variable per-token cost and better latency isolation. The uplift is workload dependent	for heavy concurrency it often reduces overall cost because you avoid multi-tenant queueing overhead. We'll include a pricing sketch.
[05:42] Roberto Diaz: For the benchmark we'd like to measure two things: time-to-first-token (TTFT) and sustained tokens/sec under batch. Can you instrument both?
[05:50] Marcus Lee: Yes, harness reports TTFT, time-to-last-token, tokens/sec, and end-to-end latency percentiles. It also exports traces you can plug into your dashboards.
[06:01] Samir Patel: Are there common gotchas? For example, do you see tail spikes because of GC or model reloads?
[06:07] Marcus Lee: Main gotchas: cold KV cache, model checkpoint swaps under high load (we lock model residency for Dedicated), and suboptimal chunk sizes for streaming. Also client-side timeouts sometimes kill streams early and look like failures. We'll walk through recommended client timeouts.
[06:22] Lena Morales: About concurrency	200-500 concurrent streaming sessions, peak 2x for flash events. Will Redwood autoscale on Hosted to absorb spikes?
[06:31] Alyssa Chen: Hosted supports autoscaling and burst capacity, but very sharp spikes can cause short-lived queueing; we can configure reserved capacity or Dedicated burst options if you need hard SLOs.
[06:44] Samir Patel: For the benchmarking, is there an easy way to include our auth & SSO flow? We want to test full production path.
[06:50] Marcus Lee: The harness can run behind your private endpoint or via short-lived tokens. For Private deployments we instrument within your VPC for full realism. For Hosted we recommend a proxy layer to simulate auth if you don't want to expose credentials.
[07:03] Roberto Diaz: Let's talk about tokenization differences	sometimes tokenizer mismatch causes length variance. Do you recommend a specific tokenizer and padding strategy for benchmarks?
[07:10] Marcus Lee: Use the tokenizer we ship with the model bundle to ensure consistency. For streaming, we avoid aggressive padding; better to benchmark with actual tokenized lengths based on your prompt set.
[07:22] Lena Morales: We also do some reranking calls and embeddings. Any implications?
[07:26] Marcus Lee: Embeddings are throughput-oriented and scale differently	tokens/sec isn't the right metric there; QPS and batch size matter. Reranking often benefits from batching and CPU-bound stages. We'll separate those in the benchmark.
[07:39] Samir Patel: Ok. For the Hosted baseline run, what inputs do you need from us?
[07:44] Marcus Lee: Representative prompt set (CSV), expected concurrency profile (percentiles over time), target p95 numbers, and preferred model family. Also region preferences and whether streaming chunking is used.
[07:55] Samir Patel: I'll get that over. Lean on Lena to assemble the prompts.
[07:59] Lena Morales: Will do.
[08:02] Alyssa Chen: Great. Any other concerns?
[08:05] Roberto Diaz: Latency SLOs vs cost, and compliance. That's covered. Also curious about failover	if a model variant is down can Redwood route to a smaller model?
[08:14] Marcus Lee: Yes, routing policies allow fallbacks to compatible model variants; you can set cost-sensitive vs latency-sensitive policies. Fallbacks are typically to a quantized or smaller architecture.
[08:25] Samir Patel: What about metrics export? Prometheus or logs?
[08:28] Marcus Lee: We support Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, and JSON audit logs pushed to S3 or your log collector; Dedicated/Private can be configured to push to your logging infrastructure.
[08:40] Alyssa Chen: OK to summarize next steps? Marcus will share the benchmark script and infra checklist; Samir/Lena will send prompt set and concurrency profile; Redwood will run Hosted baseline and deliver p50/p95/p99 and token/sec charts.
[08:53] Samir Patel: Sounds good. One more question	do you have any quick numbers for token/sec on quantized 4-bit models for batch jobs?
[09:00] Marcus Lee: Rough ballpark: quantized 4-bit can improve memory footprint and allow denser batching; tokens/sec depends on kernel support but we often see 1.5x-2x speedup for throughput workloads compared to fp16 on the same hardware, though decoding quality and latency can differ. We'll include model-specific numbers.
[09:20] Lena Morales: Perfect. That's all from me.
[09:23] Alyssa Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with artifacts and proposed dates for the baseline run.
[09:28] Samir Patel: Thanks.
[09:30] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings and speaker label swaps. The file includes action items and next steps above.
